artifact.code:
import pandas as pd

homes = pd.read_csv("eastville_teaching.csv")
homes["price"] = pd.to_numeric(
    homes["price"].str.replace("$", "", regex=False).str.replace(",", "", regex=False)
)

print("Homes on the Eastville market:", len(homes))
print()
print("Homes per school zone:")
print(homes.groupby("school")["price"].count())
print()
print("Average price by school zone:")
print(homes.groupby("school")["price"].mean().round(0))

answer_key.flaw: len(homes) counts ROWS, and this file's rows are listings: several homes were relisted and appear twice. The headline 'homes on the market' figure, the per-zone counts, and the zone averages all weight those relisted homes double. Nothing in the code checked rows against distinct house ids before claiming a count of homes.
answer_key.mechanism: A row is a record, not necessarily a thing. When the same house appears under two listings, every count and every average silently treats it as two houses. The one-line check -- compare len(homes) with homes['house'].nunique() -- was never run.
answer_key.consequence: The market looks bigger than it is and the double-counted homes pull the zone averages toward their own prices. Inventory reports, market-share claims, and zone comparisons built on these figures are all quietly wrong.
